__data__.text: King Dasaratha, having sent his sons Bharata and Satrughna to their maternal grandfather's kingdom, began to consider appointing Rama as his successor.  He consulted with a council of princes on this matter. Meanwhile, Bharata and Satrughna, though enjoying their stay, still fondly remembered their father.  Dasaratha, in turn, missed his sons, all four of whom he loved equally.  However, Rama, a virtuous and glorious prince, brought him particular joy. Rama was described as a divine incarnation, born to vanquish the evil Ravana.  His mother, Queen Kausalya, was as proud of him as Aditi was of Indra.  Rama possessed numerous admirable qualities:  He was handsome, brave, and kind.  He remained calm and spoke gently, even when provoked.  He appreciated even small acts of kindness and readily forgave offenses.  He sought the company of wise and virtuous elders. He was eloquent, yet humble despite his strength. He was honest, respectful, and beloved by the people. Compassionate and self-controlled, Rama was a devout follower of righteous conduct.

__data__.text: Rama continued to grow in virtue and wisdom.  He spent his free time conversing with those older than him in age, wisdom, and piety.  Talented and well-spoken, he initiated conversations with others in a pleasant manner.  Though strong and valiant, he remained humble.  Truthful and learned, Rama respected his elders and was beloved by the people, whom he also loved in return.  Compassionate and in control of his anger, he was devoted to Brahmins and empathetic towards the suffering.  He was knowledgeable in righteousness, practiced self-control, and lived a life of purity.  Rama diligently fulfilled his Kshatriya duties, viewing them as a path to a heavenly reward. He avoided harmful activities and distasteful conversations, preferring instead to engage in thoughtful discussions and debates, demonstrating his eloquence.  Healthy, youthful, and articulate, Rama had a keen awareness of appropriate conduct and a deep understanding of people.  His exceptional qualities made him the favorite of the people, cherished like their very lifeblood.  Mastering all areas of knowledge, including the Vedas, he surpassed even his renowned father in archery and mystical weaponry.  Blessed and benevolent, Rama remained steadfast in truth and integrity. He was guided by the wisdom of learned Brahmins, developing a strong understanding of righteousness, prosperity, and worldly affairs.  Modest and discreet, he attracted many followers.  He was judicious in both rewarding and punishing, and discerning in his assessment of character.  Rama was adept at assembling and supporting virtuous individuals, strategic in the use of force, and knowledgeable in financial matters, both in generating revenue and appropriate expenditure.  He was well-versed in both traditional scriptures and more contemporary works, balancing worldly enjoyment with righteous conduct and financial responsibility, all while remaining actively engaged in his duties.

__data__.text: Rama possessed unwavering devotion and a stable mind. He surrounded himself with worthy individuals and spoke with integrity.  He was diligent and ever watchful, discerning the strengths and weaknesses of both his own people and others.  Skilled in sacred texts, he recognized and appreciated the contributions of others.  He was a keen judge of character and dispensed justice and favor fairly.  Rama excelled at assembling and supporting virtuous individuals, strategically applying force when necessary.  He was adept at generating revenue without undue burden on the people and managing finances responsibly, adhering to established principles.  Proficient in both traditional scriptures and contemporary works, he balanced worldly enjoyment with righteous conduct and financial responsibility, remaining actively engaged in his duties.  He appreciated the arts and allocated resources wisely. Skilled in horsemanship and managing elephants, Rama was a master archer, respected even by the most formidable warriors. He was adept at both offensive and defensive warfare, strategically deploying his forces. Respected in all realms, Rama was likened to the earth in forbearance and to the preceptor of the gods in wisdom, while his valor rivaled that of Indra. The earth desired him as her protector, and his father, King Dasaratha, contemplated how to crown him while still alive, recognizing Rama's superior qualities and the people's affection for him.  Dasaratha longed to witness this event, understanding Rama's compassion for all beings and his dedication to the welfare of the people.

__data__.text: King Dasaratha contemplated crowning his son, Rama, while he was still alive.  He yearned to witness this joyous occasion, recognizing Rama's exceptional qualities, which surpassed even his own. Rama was beloved by the people, compassionate to all beings, and dedicated to their welfare.  He was compared to Yama and Indra in valor, Brihaspati in wisdom, and a mountain in steadfastness.  The king desired to see Rama ruling the world before he himself passed away.  Considering Rama's numerous virtues, Dasaratha consulted with his ministers and decided to appoint Rama as Prince Regent.  He informed them of the ominous portents he had observed and the effects of his advancing age.  However, the ministers assured him of Rama's immense popularity, which eased the king's anxieties.  Driven by his love for his people and their well-being, Dasaratha urged his ministers to expedite the coronation.  He summoned prominent citizens and rulers from across the kingdom, welcoming them with honors and gifts.  In his haste, he decided to inform King Kekaya and King Janaka later.  As Dasaratha took his seat in the assembly, the invited kings entered and sat respectfully facing him.  Surrounded by these dignitaries, King Dasaratha shone like Indra among the gods.

__data__.text: King Daśaratha, after addressing the assembly regarding Rama's appointment as Prince Regent, instructed Sage Vasiṣṭha to oversee the necessary preparations.  Vasiṣṭha, in turn, directed the ministers to gather materials for the ceremony, including gold, herbs, flowers, food, cloth, weapons, an army, an elephant, whisks, fans, a flag, a white umbrella, golden pitchers, a bull, a lion skin, and sandal paste. The king further ordered the decoration of the city and palace with garlands and incense. He also commanded that a feast be prepared for the Brahmins, along with generous gifts. Preparations were to be made for a ritual invocation of blessings the next morning, and the main road was to be sprinkled with water.  Dancers were to be stationed in the palace courtyard, ready to perform.  Shrines throughout the city were to be honored with offerings of food and money.  Armed guards, dressed in clean uniforms, were to secure the palace courtyard.  Vasiṣṭha and Vamadeva oversaw these preparations and informed the king of their completion.  Daśaratha then dispatched Sumantra to bring Rama to him.

__data__.text: King Daśaratha, deeply moved by Rama's respectful demeanor, embraced his son and offered him a magnificent gem-encrusted seat.  As Rama sat, his presence illuminated the court.  The King, filled with joy, formally addressed Rama, comparing their relationship to that of the sage Kasyapa and Indra. He declared Rama his beloved son and heir, born of his worthiest wife, Kausalya, and praised Rama's virtues, which had won the hearts of the people.  Daśaratha then advised Rama to accept the role of Prince Regent. The King, though recognizing Rama's inherent goodness, offered fatherly counsel, urging him to cultivate humility, control his desires and anger, and avoid vices. He emphasized the importance of ruling justly, both directly and through advisors, and of ensuring the kingdom's prosperity by accumulating resources and caring for his subjects. He reminded Rama that a benevolent ruler, who cherishes his people, earns the loyalty and joy of his friends and allies.  Rama's friends, eager to share the good news, rushed to Queen Kausalya and informed her of Rama's appointment.  The Queen, overjoyed, rewarded the messengers generously. Rama, after paying his respects to the King, returned to his palace, greeted by cheering crowds along the way.

He expresses joy at having a son like Rama and having fulfilled his duties to gods, sages, ancestors, and Brahmins. Now, he desires only to see Rama installed as regent. __data__.text: After priestly duties, Rama, focused in mind, worshipped Lord Narayana with Sita.  He reverently offered ghee into the sacred fire and partook of the remaining offering.  Rama then rested on a bed of kusa grass in the temple, contemplating the divine presence.  Awakening before dawn, he oversaw the temple's decoration.  Amidst the melodious recitations of storytellers, genealogists, and bards, Rama completed his morning prayers with deep concentration. Dressed in fine silk, he honored Lord Vishnu and requested blessings from the Brahmins.  The sound of these blessings, accompanied by music, filled Ayodhya.  The citizens rejoiced upon hearing of Rama's fasting and, with the arrival of dawn, began decorating the city in anticipation of his installation.  Flags and banners adorned temples, crossroads, shops, homes, and prominent trees.  The people enjoyed performances by actors, dancers, and musicians.  Conversations throughout the city centered on the upcoming installation of Rama.

The citizens, eager for Rama's installation, gathered and praised King Dasaratha for his decision.  They spoke of Dasaratha's wisdom and Rama's virtues: his humility, knowledge, piety, and love for his brothers and the people.  They expressed gratitude that Rama would be their protector. People from the countryside, drawn by the news, flocked to Ayodhya to witness the event, adding to the city's swelling population.  The noise of the crowd echoed like the roar of the ocean at high tide.

__data__.text: Manthara, a maid-servant originally from Kaikeyi’s parents' household, happened to climb onto the palace roof. From this vantage point, she observed the bustling city of Ayodhya.  The main streets were watered and adorned with flowers.  Banners and flags decorated the buildings.  The city, sprinkled with sandalwood water, teemed with people who had bathed for the special occasion.  Brahmins carrying flowers and sweets added to the festive atmosphere.  Temples with gleaming white doorways stood amongst the sounds of music and Vedic chants.  Joyful citizens, elephants, horses, and even the calls of bulls and cows contributed to the vibrant scene.  Overwhelmed by the joyous spectacle, Manthara spotted Kausalya, Rama's mother, dressed in white silk and radiating happiness.  She asked Kausalya’s old nurse why the queen, usually careful with her wealth, was so generously distributing riches. She also inquired about the cause of the widespread celebration and the king’s plans.  The nurse excitedly explained that King Dasharatha was going to install Rama as Prince Regent the following day, under the auspicious asterism of Pusya.  Upon hearing this news, Manthara became instantly enraged.  She descended from the roof and, seething with anger, approached Kaikeyi, who was resting.  Manthara urgently roused Kaikeyi, warning her of impending danger and the fleeting nature of her perceived good fortune.

She expresses concern for Bharata, highlighting the equal claim he has to the throne, and noting the loyalty of Lakshmana to Rama and Shatrughna to Bharata. Manthara points out that Bharata is the rightful heir based on seniority.  She fears Rama's capabilities as a Kshatriya, predicting his potential threat to Bharata. Manthara foresees Kausalya's rise to prominence and Kaikeyi's subservience to her, along with Bharata becoming Rama's servant. She concludes by painting a bleak picture of the future, where Rama's household will rejoice while Bharata's family suffers.  Despite Manthara's harsh words, Kaikeyi continues to praise Rama's virtues, asserting that his qualities make him deserving of the position of Prince Regent, and expressing confidence in his ability to protect his family.

__data__.text: Dasaratha, accompanied by Kaikeyi and other royal sages, journeyed south to the Dandaka forest to aid Indra in a war against the demons.  Their target was the city of Vaijayanta, ruled by the formidable demon Timidhwaja, also known as Sambara.  Sambara, a master of illusion, proved a challenging adversary, even for the gods.  The demons employed a ruthless tactic, attacking wounded and sleeping soldiers at night. During the fierce battle, Dasaratha was severely injured.  Kaikeyi bravely rescued the unconscious king from the battlefield, moving him to safety.  Grateful for her courage and quick action, Dasaratha offered Kaikeyi two boons.  Manthara reminds Kaikeyi of these unclaimed boons, urging her to use them to secure Bharata's ascension to the throne and Rama's exile. Manthara advises Kaikeyi to feign anger and refuse all other offerings from the king, emphasizing Dasaratha's deep affection for her and his willingness to fulfill her desires.

He found her chamber opulent, filled with the sounds of music and the presence of birds and servants. However, Kaikeyi was not in her usual place. Instead, she lay on the floor of her sulking-chamber, dressed in soiled clothes, her hair in a single braid, and stripped of her ornaments, which lay scattered around her.  Distressed by her unusual state, Dasaratha questioned the portress, who informed him of Kaikeyi's retreat to the sulking-chamber in anger. The king, deeply troubled, went to her and, seeing her distraught condition, tried to comfort her, inquiring about the cause of her distress and offering to fulfill any wish she might have, reminding her of his devotion and the vastness of his kingdom as proof of his ability to grant her desires. He urged her to rise and tell him what was troubling her, promising to dispel her fears as the sun dispels mist.

Dasharatha berates himself for his blindness to Kaikeyi's true nature, comparing her to poisoned wine. He feels betrayed and manipulated, likening her soothing words to a hunter's deceptive melody. The king anticipates the public shame and condemnation he will face for exiling his beloved son. He accepts responsibility for his predicament, viewing it as karmic retribution.  Dasharatha reflects on his naive trust in Kaikeyi, comparing it to a child unknowingly playing with a venomous snake.  He believes the world will rightly criticize him for failing to protect Rama. He laments that Rama, despite his noble nature and obedience, will meekly accept his unjust exile.  Finally, Dasharatha foresees his own death from the unbearable grief, predicting his demise will be met with public scorn.

He predicts a mass exodus from Ayodhya, as people follow Rama into exile, leaving the kingdom desolate.  He expresses the joy Rama's presence brings him, contrasting it with the despair he feels at the prospect of Rama's departure. Dasharatha declares that life in Ayodhya would be impossible without Rama, even if natural order itself were disrupted. He likens Kaikeyi to a deadly serpent he unknowingly harbored, a hostile enemy disguised as a loved one. He bitterly suggests she rule the kingdom with Bharata after he and his favored sons are gone, leaving her to gloat over her victory.  Dasharatha expresses surprise that Kaikeyi’s cruel words haven't caused her teeth to shatter, given the injustice of her demands. He points out Rama's gentle nature, incapable of harsh words, asking how she could find fault with such a virtuous son. He declares he will never agree to her demands, even if she resorts to self-harm, calling her a disgrace to her family.  Finally, Dasharatha begs Kaikeyi for mercy, touching her feet, pleading that his life is meaningless without Rama.

She emphasized the importance of truthfulness, citing examples of King Saibya, King Alarka, and the ocean, all of whom adhered strictly to their vows. The king’s face paled, his heart agitated, his eyes dimmed with distress.  With great effort, he finally spoke, disowning Kaikeyi, her son Bharata, and the hand he had once held in marriage, blaming her for this agonizing situation.  He lamented the approaching dawn, knowing the people eagerly awaited Rama's installation as Prince Regent.

__data__.text: As King Dasaratha grappled with Kaikeyi’s cruel demand, he felt trapped and agitated, like a bullock caught between a cart’s wheels.  His face paled, and his vision blurred with distress.  With immense effort, he rebuked Kaikeyi, disowning her, Bharata, and their marriage, placing the blame for this torment squarely on her.  He lamented the approaching dawn, knowing the populace eagerly anticipated Rama’s installation.  He proposed a morbid plan: if he couldn't bear this grief, Rama should perform his last rites using the very items meant for his coronation. Furthermore, if Rama’s installation was indeed canceled as per her wish, neither Kaikeyi nor Bharata should participate in his last rites. Dasaratha expressed his anguish at seeing his people’s joy turn to despair if Rama were not crowned.  As the night ended and dawn broke, the king continued his lament.  Kaikeyi, however, remained unmoved, coldly urging him to summon Rama and install Bharata as king, exiling Rama to the forest, thus fulfilling his promise and freeing her from perceived threats.  At that moment, as the auspicious hour for the installation arrived, Sage Vasistha entered Ayodhya with his disciples, carrying the ceremonial items, unaware of the unfolding tragedy.

__data__.text: As dawn broke, the sun rising and the auspicious hour arriving, Sage Vasistha entered Ayodhya with his disciples, bearing the items for Rama's coronation. The city was decorated with colorful banners, its streets clean and filled with joyful people. Markets overflowed with goods, and the air was fragrant with incense. Ayodhya, bustling with anticipation for Rama's installation, rivaled the splendor of Indra's celestial city.  Vasistha observed the palace, adorned with flags and teeming with citizens and rural folk, graced by Brahmins and attendants. Reaching the palace, the joyful sage and his companions bypassed the crowd at the gate, where he encountered Sumantra, Dasaratha's charioteer and minister.  Vasistha informed Sumantra of his arrival and presented the ceremonial items: sacred waters, a wooden throne, various seeds and herbs, gemstones, honey, curds, ghee, grains, grass, flowers, milk, eight maidens, an elephant, a chariot, a sword, a bow, a palanquin, an umbrella, chowries, a bull, a lion, a horse, another throne, a tiger skin, fire-starting sticks, musical instruments, adorned women, Brahmins, cows, animals, birds, prominent citizens, merchants, and their followers. All these, along with numerous well-wishers, eagerly awaited Rama's installation.  Urging the king to act swiftly, Vasistha instructed Sumantra to inform Dasaratha that the auspicious moment had arrived for Rama's coronation.  Sumantra, having received Vasistha's message, re-entered the palace, praising King Dasaratha. The king's attendants, respectful and eager to please, did not hinder Sumantra, recognizing his seniority and prior permission to see the king. Unaware of Dasaratha's distress, Sumantra approached him, intending to offer words of praise.  He began by comparing the king's joy to the ocean illuminated by the rising sun and urged him to share his happiness.  He then likened his role to that of the Vedas and other branches of knowledge guiding Brahma in creation, and to the sun and moon awakening the earth, encouraging Dasaratha to fulfill his duty.  Finally, Sumantra implored the king to rise, adorned and radiant, like the sun ascending Mount Meru.

__data__.text: Sumantra, entering a gate guarded by loyal men, proceeded to another secured by devoted guards.  He requested them to inform Rama of his arrival. The guards promptly relayed the message to Rama, who was with Sita.  Rama graciously welcomed Sumantra into his private chamber.  Sumantra found Rama, radiant and adorned, seated on a golden couch.  Sita stood beside him. Sumantra respectfully greeted Rama. He then conveyed Dasaratha's wish, along with Kaikeyi's, for Rama to see them. Rama, pleased,  conjectured to Sita that his parents' summons likely pertained to his imminent appointment as Prince Regent.

__data__.text: Sumantra informed Rama of his father Dasaratha's and Queen Kaikeyi's desire to see him. He expressed his confidence that Kaikeyi, perceptive and eager to please Dasaratha, was likely advocating for him. After bidding a loving farewell to Sita, who expressed her wishes to see him installed and offered prayers for his protection, Rama left his residence with Sumantra. __data__.text: As Rama departed the palace, blessings were invoked for his protection.  He then emerged like a lion from its mountain lair and saw Lakshmana waiting respectfully. After exchanging greetings with friends and relatives gathered at the middle gate, Rama boarded his magnificent chariot, radiant as fire.  The chariot, adorned with gold and jewels, was drawn by powerful horses and sped forth like Indra's own.  Lakshmana followed closely, holding a ceremonial fan.  The crowd erupted in cheers as Rama's procession, including elephants and warriors, moved through the city.  Musicians played, bards sang praises, and women showered flowers from balconies, expressing their joy and offering blessings.  They anticipated Kausalya's happiness at seeing Rama's impending coronation. They praised Sita's virtue, comparing her fortunate union with Rama to Rohini's with the moon god.  Amidst the celebratory clamor, Rama heard the people's enthusiastic discussions about his lineage and their hopes for his reign. They believed his rule would bring prosperity and happiness to the kingdom.  The procession continued, led by those proclaiming blessings and reciting Rama's lineage, accompanied by musicians.  Rama observed the bustling streets, filled with people, animals, chariots, and shops overflowing with goods.

__data__.text: Rama, joyous amongst his friends and family, rode his chariot through Ayodhya.  The city was decorated with flags and banners, fragrant with incense, and filled with people.  He proceeded down the main road, lined with white houses that resembled clouds.  Like Indra, king of the gods, Rama surveyed the route, clear of any danger and bustling with shops overflowing with sandalwood, aloe, silks, pearls, crystals, flowers, and food.  The crossroads were adorned with offerings.  As he passed, people called out blessings and praises, which Rama received graciously.  They spoke of the righteous path of his ancestors and expressed their hopes for even greater prosperity under his rule, surpassing even the golden age of his father, Dasaratha.  They declared that nothing would bring them more joy than Rama's coronation.  Though the crowds lauded him, Rama remained humble, yet no one could tear their gaze away from him as he passed.  Those who missed seeing him felt a pang of regret.  Rama, compassionate to all, regardless of their social standing, earned the devotion of the people.

__data__.text: Rama approached his father, King Dasaratha, who sat dejectedly with Kaikeyi.  Rama bowed respectfully to both. Dasaratha, tearful and distressed, could barely acknowledge Rama's presence.  Observing his father's unusual state, Rama became apprehensive, like one who accidentally steps on a snake. He saw the king emaciated with grief, sighing, and looking like a turbulent ocean, a sun in eclipse, or a sage who has uttered falsehood.  Concerned, Rama wondered why his father, usually so affectionate, was unresponsive. He questioned Kaikeyi, asking if he had unknowingly offended his father and pleading with her to intervene on his behalf. He expressed his deep concern for Dasaratha's well-being, hoping he was not suffering from physical or mental anguish, and anxiously inquired if he had offended Bharata, Shatrughna, or any of his mothers. Rama declared that he could not bear to live if he had displeased his father in any way.

__data__.text: Rama, deeply concerned by his father's silence and distress, questioned Kaikeyi about the cause.  He expressed his worry, hoping no physical or mental ailment troubled the king, and wondered if he had unknowingly offended anyone, including Bharata, Shatrughna, or any of his mothers.  Rama affirmed his devotion to his father, emphasizing the impossibility of living if he had caused displeasure. He wondered if Kaikeyi had perhaps spoken harshly to Dasaratha, causing him distress.  In response, Kaikeyi claimed the king was neither angry nor in anguish but held something back for fear of hurting Rama. She insisted that Rama must fulfill a promise Dasaratha made to her, a boon the king now regretted granting.  Kaikeyi implied this undisclosed promise was difficult for Dasaratha to honor and warned that the king might forsake truth due to his anger towards her for Rama's sake. She agreed to reveal the matter only if Rama pledged to obey the king's command, whatever it may be.

__data__.text: Kaikeyi continued to manipulate Rama, asserting that Dasaratha, bound by truth and piety, was tormented by the promise he made to her. She pressed Rama to swear obedience to his father's command before she would reveal it, insinuating that the king's distress stemmed from his reluctance to burden Rama with this difficult request.  Rama, distraught by the implication of his father's unhappiness, readily agreed, declaring his unwavering devotion and willingness to obey any command, even if it meant self-sacrifice. He implored Kaikeyi to disclose the king's wish.  Kaikeyi then revealed her demand: that Rama be exiled to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years while Bharata be crowned king. She claimed these were the boons Dasaratha had granted her long ago, for saving his life in battle.  She insisted that honoring this promise was the only way for both Dasaratha and Rama to uphold their integrity. She portrayed the king as heartbroken over his predicament, unable even to look at Rama due to his grief over this forced exile.

__data__.text: Kaikeyi commands Rama to relinquish his claim to the throne and instead allow Bharata to be crowned king, using the resources gathered for Rama's own coronation. She dictates that Rama must spend fourteen years in the Dandaka forest, wearing matted hair and bark clothing, while Bharata rules the prosperous kingdom.  Kaikeyi manipulates Rama by claiming that Dasaratha is overwhelmed with grief over this situation, brought about by boons he had previously granted her. She asserts that Dasaratha is unable to face Rama due to his sorrow and that fulfilling her request is the only way to uphold both his and Rama's honor.  Kaikeyi urges Rama to obey his father's supposed wish and release him from this supposed suffering.  Despite Kaikeyi's harsh words, Rama remains composed, while Dasaratha, though strong-willed, is deeply distressed by the impending separation from his son.

__data__.text: Rama, unfazed by the harsh decree, calmly accepted his exile to the forest, honoring his father's promise. He questioned Kaikeyi, seeking to understand the king's sudden change in demeanor.  Rama assured her that he bore no ill will and would willingly obey, even relinquishing Sita and his own life if commanded. He emphasized his eagerness to fulfill his father's wishes, especially if it pleased Kaikeyi.  Concerned by the king's sadness, Rama urged that messengers be sent to retrieve Bharata.  He affirmed his resolve to depart swiftly for the Dandaka forest, adhering to his father's command without question.  Pleased with his compliance, Kaikeyi hastened his departure, promising to summon Bharata. She dismissed Rama's concerns about the king's silence, attributing it to shyness and urging him to disregard it.

Dasaratha, heartbroken by Rama's words, collapsed onto his couch, overcome with grief.  Rama, urged by Kaikeyi, prepared to leave for the forest.  He responded to Kaikeyi's harsh words by stating his disinterest in worldly possessions and his commitment to righteousness.  He affirmed his duty to his father and agreed to his fourteen-year exile. He then requested permission to bid farewell to his mother, Kausalya, and Sita before departing for the Dandaka forest.  He reminded Kaikeyi of her duty to ensure Bharata's proper governance of the kingdom and care for their father. Dasaratha, unable to speak, wept aloud in his anguish.

Rama, after paying his respects to his father and Kaikeyi, departed.  Leaving the inner quarters, he met his friends.  A visibly upset Lakshmana, followed close behind.  Rama, bypassing the consecration preparations, maintained his composure despite the loss of his kingship.  He dismissed his attendants and, controlling his emotions, entered his mother's chambers to convey the unwelcome news. Despite the circumstances, Rama's outward appearance remained unchanged, showing no visible sign of distress.  He maintained his usual joyful demeanor and respectful manner as he entered his mother's presence, followed by Lakshmana, who also struggled to contain his sorrow.

__data__.text: As Rama left Kaikeyi's palace, the women inside cried out, lamenting his imminent departure. They praised his virtues, recalling how he cared for them, protected them, and resolved their disputes peacefully.  Meanwhile, King Dasaratha, overcome with shame and sorrow at his decision, hid himself.  Rama, though deeply saddened by the grief of his loved ones, proceeded with Lakshmana to his mother Kausalya's quarters.  He passed the gatekeepers, who greeted him with cheers, then the Brahmins at the second gate, and finally the women and guards at the third gate.  The women joyfully informed Kausalya of Rama's arrival.  Kausalya, who had spent the night in prayer and was continuing her rituals at daybreak, offering oblations to Vishnu, was unaware of the events that had transpired.

__data__.text: At the third gate of Kausalya's palace, Rama saw women, young girls, and elderly men guarding the entrance.  The women, excited about Rama's supposed appointment as crown prince, rushed inside to share the good news with his mother.  Meanwhile, Kausalya, unaware of the recent events, had spent the night in prayer and continued her morning rituals, offering oblations to Vishnu. Dressed in silk and dedicated to religious practices, she oversaw the priests as they chanted sacred texts and poured offerings into the fire.  Rama entered his mother's chambers and saw the preparations for the divine worship: curds, rice, ghee, sweetmeats, parched paddy, white flowers, a rice pudding, sesame rice, sacrificial wood, and water-filled jars. He observed his mother, pale from fasting, as she performed the rites.  Kausalya, overjoyed to see her son after a long time, rushed to greet him as a mare greets her foal.  Rama embraced his mother.

Rama, however, gently corrected this misunderstanding, revealing his impending fourteen-year exile to the Dandaka forest. He explained that he would live like an ascetic, subsisting on roots, fruits, and other forest fare, while Bharata would be crowned Prince Regent.  Kausalya, devastated by this news, collapsed like a felled tree.  Rama comforted his grieving mother, brushing the dust from her clothes.  Kausalya lamented her fate, expressing that the pain of separation from her son was far greater than the sorrow of childlessness. She further worried about the unkind words she would endure from her co-wives due to Rama's exile.

He argued against Rama's exile, questioning Dasaratha's decision to banish his eldest son due to Kaikeyi's influence. Lakshmana couldn't fathom any wrongdoing on Rama's part that merited such punishment, asserting that no one, not even Rama's enemies, could find fault with him.  He criticized Dasaratha for succumbing to Kaikeyi's will, likening the king's behavior to that of a senile man driven by desire.  Lakshmana questioned how any virtuous person could exile such a noble son. He then proposed that Rama seize control of the kingdom before the news of the exile spread, offering his unwavering support and protection. Lakshmana declared he would eliminate anyone who opposed Rama, including those loyal to Bharata.  He even suggested that Dasaratha should face consequences if he sided with Kaikeyi against Rama.  Finally, Lakshmana challenged Dasaratha's authority to bestow the kingdom upon Bharata, questioning his right to create such conflict.

Trijata, wearing a tattered loincloth, made his way to Rama's palace, his spiritual presence evident.  He appealed to Rama, highlighting his poverty and many children. Rama playfully challenged Trijata, offering him as many cows as he could encompass with a throw of his staff.  Trijata, invigorated, threw his staff with all his might. The staff flew across the Sarayu River and landed near a bull amidst a vast herd of grazing cows.  Honoring the unconventional measure, Rama bestowed upon Trijata all the cows from the staff's landing point up to the riverbank.

Their weapons, carried by servants, were adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste, likely applied by Sita.  As they walked, people watched sadly from rooftops and balconies, unable to navigate the crowded streets.  They lamented Rama's exile, observing that he who once commanded armies now walked with only Sita and Lakshmana.  The people praised Rama's virtue and commitment to his father's word, despite the luxuries he was forfeiting.  They expressed sorrow for Sita, now exposed to the elements, and questioned Dasaratha's decision, believing only an evil influence could cause him to banish such a virtuous son, beloved by all.  The citizens felt Rama's loss deeply, likening it to a drought harming water creatures or damage to a tree's roots affecting the whole plant.  Some even expressed a desire to join Rama in exile.

They contrasted their willing exile with Kaikeyi's supposed enjoyment of the vacated city, describing the empty palaces as desolate and neglected.  Despite the emotional outpouring and strong words from the people, Rama remained undisturbed and continued towards his father's palace.

Dasaratha, upon their arrival, asked Sumantra to bring Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita to him.  The charioteer quickly returned with them.  Seeing Rama approach, Dasaratha rose from his seat, overwhelmed with grief, and fainted before reaching his son. Rama and Lakshmana rushed to their father's side, while the palace echoed with the cries of the women. Gently, Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita lifted the unconscious king and placed him on a couch.  When Dasaratha regained consciousness, Rama, with folded hands and tearful eyes, requested his father's permission to leave for the Dandaka forest. He also asked that Lakshmana and Sita be allowed to accompany him, despite his earlier attempts to dissuade them.  Rama implored his father to grant them leave, comparing his situation to that of Brahma granting his sons leave to pursue ascetic life in the forest.  Observing Rama patiently awaiting his approval, Dasaratha, still distraught over Kaikeyi's influence, urged Rama to take control of Ayodhya and imprison him, declaring that he had been robbed of his senses by Kaikeyi's boon.  In response, the righteous Rama respectfully addressed his father.

Rama, however, calmly requested his father's permission to fulfill his promise and depart for the forest with Sita and Lakshmana. He urged Rama to depart on an auspicious journey, acknowledging the unwavering nature of Rama's commitment. Dasaratha then pleaded with Rama to delay his departure, even just for one night, so he could find solace in his presence.  He reminded Rama of his filial duty and the difficulty of such a sacrifice. Dasaratha admitted his powerlessness against Kaikeyi's deceptive influence, lamenting that he had been manipulated into this situation. He praised Rama's nobility in upholding a forced promise. He acknowledged and appreciated Rama's unwavering commitment to truth and righteousness, even in the face of such adversity.  Overcome by grief, Dasaratha made one final plea for Rama to stay, while Rama and Lakshmana listened with distress.

__data__.text: Rama swears by his virtue and past deeds, urging his father to stay true to his word and allow him to fulfill his promise.  He insists he cannot remain home any longer and implores Dasaratha to control his grief, as there is no turning back. He reminds his father of Kaikeyi's command and his own vow to obey, emphasizing the necessity of honoring his pledge.  Rama assures his father that he will find happiness in the forest amongst the animals and nature. He reiterates his respect for his father, likening him to a deity whose commands must be obeyed.  He promises to return after fourteen years, urging Dasaratha to relinquish his sorrow.  Rama questions his father's grief, pointing out that Dasaratha should be the one offering comfort, not needing it himself.  He renounces his claim to the kingdom, suggesting that Bharata rule in his stead.  He expresses his disinterest in worldly pleasures and kingship, prioritizing obedience to his father's command above all else. He reiterates his lack of desire for the throne, the earth, or even Sita, compared to fulfilling his father’s promise to Kaikeyi.  He envisions a peaceful existence in the forest, living on fruits and roots, and asks his father to find peace in this decision.  Overcome with grief and anguish, Dasaratha faints upon hearing Rama's words. All the queens present, except Kaikeyi, begin to weep, and Sumantra also faints, leaving the scene filled with lamentations.

__data__.text: Sumantra, deeply distressed by Kaikeyi's insistence on Rama's exile, rebukes her sharply. He expresses his disapproval through his actions and words, comparing her actions to murdering her husband and destroying her family.  He questions her disregard for Dasaratha, highlighting that a husband's wishes should supersede even those of numerous sons. Sumantra emphasizes the established tradition of inheritance and criticizes Kaikeyi for disrupting it. He declares his loyalty to Rama, stating that he and others will follow Rama into exile. Sumantra condemns Kaikeyi's actions, wondering why the earth doesn't split open in response to her behavior and why the harsh words of the Brahmana sages haven't affected her. He expresses his disbelief at the impropriety of her actions, given the potential loss of support from her family and the wider community.

__data__.text: Sumantra continues his condemnation of Kaikeyi, asserting that no respectable person, let alone a Brahmana, should remain in her kingdom if she proceeds with her unjust demand to exile Rama. He declares his unwavering loyalty to Rama, stating that he and others will follow Rama into exile, leaving Kaikeyi isolated from her family, Brahmanas, and all righteous individuals. He questions what satisfaction she could possibly derive from ruling a kingdom devoid of such support.  Sumantra expresses his astonishment that the earth itself doesn't react to her appalling behavior.  He wonders why the strong rebukes of the Brahmana sages haven't swayed her from her destructive course. He then draws an analogy, comparing nurturing Kaikeyi with nurturing a Neem tree (known for its bitterness) after cutting down a mango tree (known for its sweetness).  Just as a Neem tree cannot be made sweet even with milk, Kaikeyi's inherent nature, like her mother's, is incapable of producing goodness. Sumantra recounts the story of Kaikeyi's mother and how she manipulated her husband, Dasaratha's father.  He relates how Dasaratha's father was granted the ability to understand the language of all beings and how this led to a situation where his laughter over something a bird said angered his wife. Fearful of her wrath, he initially refused to tell her the reason for his laughter but eventually confided in the sage who granted him the boon. The sage advised him not to reveal the secret, even if it meant his wife leaving him.  Sumantra uses this story to illustrate Kaikeyi's inherited tendency towards manipulative behavior and her influence on Dasaratha's current predicament.

__data__.text: Sumantra continues his impassioned plea to Kaikeyi, recounting how her father wisely heeded the advice of a sage and refused to divulge a secret to his wife, even under threat of her departure. He draws a parallel to Kaikeyi's own behavior, suggesting that she has inherited her mother's manipulative tendencies and is now leading Dasaratha down a dangerous path. He urges her to abandon her wicked advisors and uphold her husband's wishes, reminding her that Dasaratha, like the world's protector, should not be swayed into improper actions.  Sumantra emphasizes Dasaratha's unwavering commitment to his promises and advocates for Rama's rightful ascension to the throne. He warns Kaikeyi of the widespread condemnation she will face if Rama is exiled and assures her that Rama is the only suitable ruler for Ayodhya.  Finally, he predicts Dasaratha's retreat to the forest if Rama is appointed Prince Regent. Despite Sumantra's blend of gentle persuasion and sharp rebukes, Kaikeyi remains unmoved, showing no outward sign of emotion or change of heart.

__data__.text: Dasaratha, grieving over his forced promise to Kaikeyi, instructs Sumantra to prepare a grand retinue for Rama's exile.  He requests an army detachment, provisions, merchants, entertainers, and Rama's favored wrestlers to accompany him.  Dasaratha further orders that his own treasury and granaries be sent with Rama, ensuring his comfort in the forest. He envisions Rama hunting, enjoying nature, performing religious rites, and living contentedly while Bharata governs Ayodhya.  Overhearing this, Kaikeyi becomes fearful and interrupts. She declares that Bharata will not accept a kingdom stripped of its wealth, comparing it to flavorless wine.  Dasaratha, angered by her callous words, questions why she torments him further and didn't stipulate these conditions earlier. This only fuels Kaikeyi’s anger, prompting a sharp retort.

__data__.text: Kaikeyi argues that Bharata will reject a kingdom emptied of its treasury, comparing it to flavorless wine.  Dasaratha, in growing frustration, questions Kaikeyi's cruel timing, asking why she didn't specify these conditions earlier.  Infuriated, Kaikeyi retorts by citing the example of King Sagara who banished his eldest son, Asamanja.  She insists Rama should similarly be sent away with nothing. Dasaratha, ashamed by her comparison, exclaims, “Shame!”  A sentiment echoed by the onlookers. Undeterred, Kaikeyi remains firm in her resolve.  The respected minister, Siddhartha, intervenes, reminding Kaikeyi of Asamanja's wickedness:  He threw children playing in the streets into the Sarayu river for his amusement. The terrified citizens begged Sagara to choose between them and his cruel son.  Sagara, heeding his people's pleas, banished Asamanja, providing him with only basic tools for survival. Siddhartha emphasizes Asamanja's deserved punishment for his cruel actions and contrasts it with Rama's impeccable character, asking what wrong Rama has committed to warrant such harsh treatment.  He concludes by stating that finding a fault in Rama is as impossible as finding a blemish on the new moon.

__data__.text: Siddhartha continues his argument against Rama's exile. He recounts Asamanja's banishment, highlighting that the king's son was provided with basic necessities – a spade and basket – for his survival in the wilderness.  Siddhartha then pointedly asks what wrong Rama has committed to justify such a severe punishment, emphasizing Rama's flawless character and the impossibility of finding fault with him, comparing it to finding a blemish on the new moon. He implores Kaikeyi to state Rama's transgression, assuring her that if a valid reason is presented, Rama will be exiled. Siddhartha argues that exiling the innocent and righteous Rama would be a grave injustice, detrimental even to the most powerful. He cautions Kaikeyi against such an action, warning that public condemnation will surely follow.  Overhearing this exchange, a grief-stricken Dasaratha, his voice weakened with sorrow, reproaches Kaikeyi for her callous decision. He questions her understanding of his and her own well-being, lamenting her unwise choice and its deviation from righteousness. Dasaratha declares his intention to relinquish his kingdom and all its comforts to accompany Rama into exile, urging Kaikeyi to rule with Bharata.

__data__.text: Upon hearing the chief minister's objection, Rama politely addressed King Dasaratha, stating that an army was unnecessary for his forest exile, as he intended to live off the land. He compared clinging to an army after relinquishing royal comforts to keeping an elephant's tether after giving the elephant away.  Rama requested simple forest attire from Kaikeyi's servants. Kaikeyi herself, shamelessly presented Rama and Lakshmana with bark garments before the assembled crowd.  Rama and Lakshmana accepted the bark clothing and exchanged their princely robes for the ascetic garb.  Sita, accustomed to silk, was distressed by the rough bark clothing.  Overwhelmed and unsure how to wear it, she fumbled with the unfamiliar material.  Rama, ever compassionate, helped her don the bark garment over her silken clothes.

__data__.text: Sita, unfamiliar with forest attire, struggled to put on the bark garment.  She fumbled with the pieces, feeling embarrassed by her inexperience.  Rama, ever mindful of others' needs, gently helped her drape the bark cloth over her silken dress.  Witnessing this, the women of the palace wept, lamenting Sita's undeserved exile.  They pleaded with Rama to leave Sita behind, arguing that she was not obligated to share his hardship. They urged him to go with Lakshmana alone, while Sita remained in the comfort of the palace.  Despite their heartfelt pleas, Rama continued to secure Sita's bark garment, mirroring her quiet acceptance of the situation.  Vasistha, observing this exchange, intervened.  He rebuked Kaikeyi for her heartless actions, declaring that Sita would not go into exile.  He asserted that Sita, as Rama's wife, would remain and assume the throne. Vasistha prophesied that if Sita accompanied Rama, the entire kingdom – people, resources, and even the city itself – would follow them into the forest. He further predicted that Bharata and Shatrughna would also join Rama in his forest exile, emulating his ascetic life.

__data__.text: King Dasaratha, grieved by the public outcry against Sita's exile, laments his powerlessness.  He rebukes Kaikeyi, arguing that the delicate, young Sita, accustomed to comfort, doesn't deserve such harsh treatment. He questions why the innocent princess is being forced to wear bark clothing like a common hermit. Dasaratha insists that Sita should not be subject to this exile, reminding Kaikeyi that his original promise only concerned Rama. He feels his rash oath and Kaikeyi's subsequent actions, particularly forcing this humiliation upon Sita, will be his ruin.  He asks Kaikeyi what wrong Sita, gentle and kind, has ever done her.  Dasaratha pleads with her to be satisfied with Rama's exile and not compound her sins by exiling Sita as well. He reminds her that he only agreed to Rama's exile, not Sita's.  As Rama departs for the forest, he addresses his dejected father, asking him to care for his kind and elderly mother, Kausalya, who has always spoken well of him.

__data__.text: King Dasharatha, overcome with grief upon seeing Rama dressed as a hermit, fainted.  He was unable to bear the sight of his son in such a state.  Upon regaining consciousness, the king lamented his past actions, believing his current misfortune to be a karmic consequence.  Despite his immense sorrow, he acknowledged that life and death are governed by fate.  He blamed Kaikeyi for the family's suffering, attributing her selfish motives to the present crisis.  Overwhelmed with emotion, Dasharatha managed to utter Rama's name once before being overcome by tears.  He then instructed Sumantra to prepare a chariot and escort Rama out of the kingdom. Lamenting the injustice of a virtuous son being exiled by his own parents, Dasharatha summoned the treasurer and ordered him to provide Sita with fine clothing and jewels befitting her station and the duration of her exile.

__data__.text: Kausalya advised Sita, emphasizing that a husband should be the most sacred figure in a virtuous woman's life.  She urged Sita not to despise Rama due to his exile, reminding her that he remains her divine consort regardless of their circumstances. Sita respectfully assured Kausalya that she understood her wifely duties and would remain devoted to Rama. She declared her inability to stray from virtue, comparing it to the moon's inseparable connection to its light. Sita used metaphors to illustrate her point, stating a vina is useless without strings, a chariot without wheels, and a woman without a husband cannot find happiness, even with many sons. She affirmed that a husband provides unmatched joy, surpassing the happiness offered by parents, siblings, or children.  Sita reiterated her understanding of wifely dharma (duty) and questioned how she could possibly disregard her husband.  Kausalya, deeply moved by Sita's words, wept with a mixture of sorrow and joy.  Observing his mother's distress, Rama comforted her, promising that their exile would end soon and they would return to Ayodhya. He then addressed his stepmothers, asking for their forgiveness for any past transgressions and bidding them farewell.  His words, full of respect and righteousness, resonated with the grieving women.

__data__.text: Rama, Sita, and a grieving Lakshmana circled King Dasaratha, touching his feet as a mark of respect before their departure.  After taking leave of the king, Rama, accompanied by Sita, bowed to his mother, Kausalya. Lakshmana also paid his respects to Kausalya and then to his own mother, Sumitra.  A weeping Sumitra embraced Lakshmana, advising him to faithfully serve his elder brother Rama during their exile. She emphasized that Rama should be his sole refuge and guide, reminding him of their family's tradition of service and sacrifice. Sumitra blessed both Rama and Lakshmana for their journey.  She told Lakshmana to consider Rama as his father, Sita as his mother, and the forest as their home.  Sumantra, the charioteer, respectfully addressed Rama, urging him to board the chariot and promising a swift journey. He reminded Rama that the fourteen-year exile, decreed by Kaikeyi, began that day.  A joyful Sita, adorned with gifts from Dasaratha, then ascended the sun-like chariot.

As Rama's chariot departed, the citizens of Ayodhya mourned deeply. They praised Sita's unwavering devotion to her husband, comparing her to a shadow that never leaves its source or the sun's light that perpetually graces Mount Meru.  They commended Lakshmana's wisdom and loyalty in choosing to accompany his brother, recognizing the great fortune and spiritual merit in serving the kind-hearted Rama.  Overcome with emotion, they followed the chariot, tears streaming down their faces.

King Dasaratha, heartbroken and surrounded by his grieving wives, left the palace, determined to see his son one last time. The cries of the women filled the air, echoing the distress of elephants separated from their leader.  Dasaratha, once radiant, now appeared diminished, like the moon eclipsed by Rahu.  Meanwhile, Rama, resolute and composed, urged Sumantra to hasten their departure.  Torn between Rama's command to proceed and the pleas of the citizens to stop, Sumantra could only continue onward. The dust raised by the chariot wheels settled, dampened by the citizens' tears.  The people of Ayodhya, overwhelmed by sorrow, wept and fainted as they watched their beloved prince leave.  Tears flowed from the women's eyes like water droplets from disturbed lotus blossoms. Witnessing the collective grief of his city, Dasaratha collapsed like a felled tree.  A great cry arose from those following Rama as they saw the king's anguish.  Some called out to Rama, others to his mother, Kausalya, who was also following the chariot, her heart filled with sorrow. Rama, glancing back, saw his father's despair and his mother's grief.

The ministers advised the king against following any further, saying it was unwise to pursue someone you wished to see return.  Overwhelmed with grief and exhaustion, Dasaratha finally stopped, watching his son depart with a heavy heart, accompanied by his equally distressed wives.

As the dust disappeared, marking Rama's increasing distance, the King collapsed to the ground in despair.  Kausalya, his chief wife, rushed to his right side to help him up, while Kaikeyi approached his left.  Seeing Kaikeyi, Dasaratha, overcome with grief and anger, rebuked her, forbidding her from touching him and disowning her as his wife and kin. He declared that he renounced any connection to her or those who served her, blaming her selfish desires and lack of virtue for Rama's exile.  He even disavowed any future benefit from their marriage rituals and declared that any offerings Bharata might make in the afterlife on his behalf should not reach him. Kausalya then lifted the dust-covered king and escorted him back to the palace.  Dasaratha, tormented by the thought of Rama's exile, felt intense remorse, like someone who had committed a terrible act. He repeatedly looked back at the path Rama's chariot had taken, his appearance as diminished as a sun in eclipse.  Anguished, the king lamented the loss of his beloved son.  Upon learning that Rama had reached the city's outskirts, he cried out that while the hoofprints of the chariot horses were still visible, Rama himself was gone from sight.

He cried out in anguish, noting that while the hoofprints of the chariot horses were still visible, Rama himself was gone.  The king imagined Rama's current hardship, contrasting it with his former comfort: how the prince, once accustomed to soft cushions, sandal paste, and gentle breezes, would now be sleeping on the bare ground, under a tree, his head resting on a rough piece of wood or stone. He pictured Rama rising at dawn, covered in dust, sighing deeply. He envisioned forest dwellers seeing the exiled prince, the protector of the world, wandering as a forlorn figure.  Dasaratha also lamented Sita's plight, imagining her delicate feet injured by thorns as she walked through the forest, and her fear upon hearing the roars of wild animals.  Turning his anger towards Kaikeyi, he blamed her for his misery, wishing her a widow's life in the kingdom he now found unbearable without Rama.  Surrounded by his people, the grieving king returned to his palace, now as desolate as a pool emptied of its life.  He looked upon the deserted city, its empty streets and closed shops, a reflection of his own despair.  Entering the palace, which felt empty without Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana, he feebly requested his attendants to take him to Kausalya, Rama's mother, seeking solace in her presence.

__data__.text: The people of Ayodhya, deeply devoted to Rama, followed him into exile.  Even when King Dasharatha returned to the city, bound by custom to only accompany Rama a short distance, the citizens refused to leave Rama's side. Rama, renowned for his virtues, was beloved by the people of Ayodhya like the full moon. Though the people pleaded with him, Rama, honoring his father's promise, continued towards the forest.  Looking at them with affection, Rama addressed the citizens, urging them to transfer their love and respect to Bharata. He assured them that Bharata, though young, possessed wisdom and noble qualities and would rule wisely, allaying their fears. Rama emphasized Bharata's suitability as a leader and urged the citizens to obey him and their father, King Dasharatha, so that the king wouldn't grieve during Rama's exile.  The more Rama adhered to his father's wishes, the stronger the people's desire for him as their king became. Rama and Lakshmana, through their virtues, drew the tearful citizens with them as if bound by cords. Elderly Brahmanas, unable to keep pace with Rama's chariot, called out, urging the horses to turn back and be loyal to their master by not taking him further against the people's wishes. They reminded the horses that all creatures, especially those with ears, heard their pleas and should therefore heed them.

They appealed to all creatures, particularly those with ears, to hear their plea and persuade Rama to return. They extolled Rama's virtues and argued that such a noble person deserved to be taken back to the city, not further into the forest. Seeing their anguish, Rama quickly descended from his chariot and began walking with Sita and Lakshmana. This gesture allowed the elderly Brahmanas to keep pace. Rama, known for his compassion, couldn't bear to ride while they struggled on foot.  Distressed by Rama's continued departure, the Brahmanas declared their unwavering devotion and intention to follow him, pointing out that even the sacred fires were being carried along. They offered their ceremonial canopies as shade from the sun and expressed their shift in focus from Vedic studies to accompanying him. Assuring Rama of their wives' safety at home, the Brahmanas questioned who would uphold righteousness if Rama, a paragon of virtue, disregarded their pleas.  Lowering their dust-covered, white-haired heads, they implored him to return.

__data__.text: The Brahmanas, deeply attached to Rama, declared their unwavering resolve to follow him into exile.  Their minds, once focused on Vedic scriptures, were now fixed on accompanying him.  They assured Rama that their wives were safe and their knowledge of the Vedas secure within their memories.  They questioned how righteousness could prevail if Rama, its embodiment, ignored their pleas.  With heads bowed low, their white hair dusted from prostration, they begged him to return.  They reminded him of the unfinished sacrifices that depended on his presence.  Even the inanimate and animate world, they asserted, yearned for his return, symbolized by the rustling leaves of trees that seemed to cry out and the motionless, hungry birds perched on branches. As this heartfelt plea continued, they reached the Tamasa River, its presence seemingly a further attempt to impede Rama's journey.  Meanwhile, Sumantra, Rama's charioteer, unyoked the weary horses, allowing them to drink, bathe, and graze near the riverbank.

metadata.canto_summary:
Canto XLVI

Having reached the bank of the Tamasa and thinking of the plight of the
people of Ayodhya, Sri Rama lays himself down on a bed of leaves
bewailing the lot of his parents and feeling reassured by the thought
of Bharata’s noble qualities; while Laksmana opens his dialogue
with Sumantra on the divine excellences of Sri Rama. Waking
up in the meantime, Sri Rama urges the charioteer-minister to
drive the chariot in such a way as to put the citizens, that
had accompanied them, off the scent and lead them to
think that the chariot had turned back towards
Ayodhya instead of proceeding towards the forest.

He then mounts the chariot alongwith Sita and
Laksmana and presses on to the forest

__data__.text: On the banks of the Tamasa river, Rama, looking at Sita, addressed Lakshmana.  He reminded Lakshmana that this was their first night of exile and urged him not to worry about those left behind in Ayodhya.  Rama observed the quiet forest, noting the animals and birds seeking shelter, and lamented that the city of Ayodhya, his father's capital, would be mourning their departure. He acknowledged the people's affection for himself, Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna. Rama expressed concern for his parents, fearing their grief might overwhelm them. However, he took comfort in Bharata's kind nature, believing he would console their parents. Rama then thanked Lakshmana for accompanying him, stating it relieved him of the burden of seeking aid to protect Sita. He declared his intention to fast that night, subsisting only on water despite the availability of wild fruits.  Rama then instructed Sumantra to attend to the horses. After Sumantra had seen to the horses’ needs, he returned to Rama.  As night fell, Sumantra and Lakshmana prepared a bed of leaves for Rama. Rama and Sita then retired for the night on the riverbank. While Rama slept, Lakshmana spoke with Sumantra about Rama's many virtues.

__data__.text: After Sumantra attended to the horses, he returned to Rama. Sumantra and Lakshmana then prepared a bed of leaves for Rama and Sita on the banks of the Tamasa river.  Rama and Sita rested there for the night.  As Rama slept, Lakshmana discussed Rama's virtues with Sumantra.  They stayed awake all night, and as the sun rose, Rama awoke to find the citizens of Ayodhya still camped nearby. He observed their devotion and instructed Lakshmana to prepare for their departure quickly while the citizens slept, choosing a safe and secluded route to minimize further hardship for the devoted people of Ayodhya. Lakshmana agreed, and Rama instructed Sumantra to prepare the chariot. Sumantra promptly readied the chariot and informed Rama, urging him to board with Sita and Lakshmana.

__data__.text: Lakshmana agreed with Rama's suggestion to depart quickly.  Rama then instructed Sumantra to prepare the chariot for their journey into the forest.  Sumantra quickly prepared the chariot and informed Rama that it was ready.  Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana boarded the chariot, and they swiftly crossed the Tamasa River.  After crossing the river, they traveled on a smooth, safe road.  To mislead the citizens of Ayodhya who had followed them, Rama instructed Sumantra to drive the chariot north for a short distance and then return discreetly, creating the impression that they were heading back to Ayodhya.  Sumantra followed Rama's instructions and reported back. Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana then settled comfortably in the chariot, and Sumantra drove them towards a forest suitable for ascetic life, initially heading north due to favorable omens.

__data__.text: The citizens who had followed Rama awoke at dawn to find him gone. Grief-stricken and tearful, they searched for him but could not even catch a glimpse. Dejected and bewildered, they lamented, "Woe to the sleep that kept us from noticing Rama's departure! How could he, whose actions are always purposeful, abandon us, his devoted followers, for a life of asceticism in the forest? He was like a father to us! Should we end our lives here or journey north to die?  What good is life without him?  We could light a funeral pyre and perish together. How can we face those in Ayodhya and tell them that we let Rama, the kind and generous, go?  The city will be devastated.  Having accompanied him, how can we return without him?"  They searched for his chariot tracks for a while, but the trail disappeared.  Disheartened and feeling abandoned by fate, they retraced their steps back to Ayodhya, where the citizens were already in despair.

__data__.text: The citizens, heartbroken like cows who have lost their calves, continued to lament Rama's departure. Following the chariot tracks for a short distance, they were dismayed when the trail vanished, realizing Rama had taken a different route back.  Discouraged and feeling abandoned by fate, they questioned what they should do, lamenting their misfortune.  With heavy hearts, they returned to Ayodhya, finding the city and its people already gripped by despair.  The city, without Rama, appeared desolate, like a river stripped of its serpents or the sky without the moon, bringing the citizens no joy.  They entered their opulent homes, yet their sorrow was so profound they could barely recognize their own families, their happiness completely gone.

__data__.text: The citizens of Ayodhya, heartbroken by Rama's departure, returned home grieving.  Their sorrow was palpable, their tears flowed freely.  Upon reaching their homes, they were met by their families, and the collective weeping intensified.  Joy vanished from the city. Merchants ceased their trade, households stopped cooking, and even the return of lost wealth or the birth of a son brought no solace.  The women of Ayodhya, distraught at Rama's absence, reproached their husbands, questioning the value of home, family, and possessions without him.  They praised Lakshmana for his unwavering loyalty in accompanying Rama and Sita.  They envied the rivers, ponds, and lakes that Rama would grace with his presence, the forests and mountains that would adorn his path.  Nature itself, they believed, would honor Rama, offering him flowers, fruits, and clear waters.  They declared that where Rama resided, fear and humiliation could not exist.

__data__.text: The women of Ayodhya continued lamenting Rama's exile.  They envisioned the beautiful flora and refreshing waters that would greet Rama on his journey, believing that nature itself would honor him.  They affirmed that wherever Rama resided, fear and disgrace could not exist.  Hope briefly flickered as they expressed a desire to follow Rama, seeking the protection and solace of his presence.  Their grief then turned to anger directed at Kaikeyi. They declared their unwillingness to live under her rule, fearing her unjust and destructive influence on the kingdom. They predicted the demise of the king and the ruin of the kingdom in Rama's absence, urging their husbands to choose death, exile with Rama, or flight to a place untouched by Kaikeyi's name, rather than endure her reign.

__data__.text: The women of Ayodhya continued to mourn Rama's exile. They questioned how anyone could find happiness under the rule of Kaikeyi, who orchestrated Rama's banishment. They lamented that the kingdom was rudderless and predicted its imminent ruin due to Kaikeyi's actions.  In their despair, they contemplated drastic measures – poison, following Rama into exile, or fleeing to a place untouched by Kaikeyi's influence.  They felt unjustly bound to Bharata's rule, comparing themselves to livestock awaiting slaughter.  Amidst their grief, they described Rama's noble qualities – his strength, his truthfulness, his gentle nature, and his striking appearance.  Their sorrow intensified as night fell, and Ayodhya, once vibrant, became shrouded in darkness and silence.  The cessation of daily activities and the absence of joy transformed the city into a desolate wasteland, mirroring the emptiness in their hearts.  Overwhelmed by grief, they wept and fainted, their love for Rama surpassing even their love for their own sons. The once joyous city became a bleak shadow of its former self, devoid of music, celebration, and prosperity.

__data__.text: Rama, obeying his father's order, journeyed a long distance through the night.  As he traveled, the pleasant night passed, and after morning prayers, he continued onward, passing through numerous regions.  He observed well-cultivated villages and blossoming forests as he rode, seemingly at a slow pace but actually covering ground quickly, thanks to his excellent horses.  He overheard the conversations of villagers, who lamented Dasaratha's decision, influenced by desire, to exile Rama. They criticized Kaikeyi for her harshness and improper actions in orchestrating Rama's banishment.  They expressed concern for Sita, accustomed to comfort, now facing hardship, and questioned Dasaratha's lack of affection in abandoning his blameless son. Rama continued his journey, passing out of Kosala, crossing the Vedasruti river, and then the Gomati, a river with cool waters and cows on its banks.  He also crossed the Syandika river, filled with the sounds of peacocks and swans.  He pointed out to Sita the prosperous land of Kosala, gifted long ago by Manu to Ikshvaku, and discussed with his charioteer Sumantra his longing to return to Ayodhya and hunt in the forests with his parents.

__data__.text: Rama, bidding farewell to Ayodhya, addressed the city, expressing his gratitude to its protectors and promising to return after his exile.  He then tearfully addressed the people who had accompanied him, requesting them to return to their homes.  The people, grieving, paid their respects and watched as Rama departed.  He journeyed through the prosperous lands of Kosala, passing through villages filled with resources, charitable people, and places of worship. He then entered a territory of contented people and abundant livestock, marked by the sounds of Vedic chants.  Continuing his journey, Rama reached the banks of the sacred river Ganga, a threefold river frequented by sages and celestial beings, adorned with hermitages and graced by the presence of various divine beings. Its pools, overflowing with water, served as a haven for celestial nymphs and its banks as a playground for gods.

__data__.text: Rama reached the divine Ganga river.  The threefold river flowed through the heavens, earth, and the underworld. Its cool, clear waters were frequented by sages.  The riverbanks, adorned with hermitages, were visited by celestial nymphs and various divine beings. The river flowed through celestial gardens and contained divine lotuses.  Its waters, sometimes calm, sometimes turbulent, created a variety of sounds.  The river, teeming with life, was graced by the presence of swans, cranes, and other birds. Its banks were lined with trees and flowers.  Purified by the touch of Vishnu's feet, the river cleansed those who bathed in or drank its waters.

__data__.text: Rama, accompanied by Sita and Lakshmana, arrived at the Ganga river. The river was described as pure, its waters capable of washing away sins. __data__.text: Guha, deeply saddened by Rama's ascetic attire, embraced him and offered his kingdom of Sragaverapura, along with various foods and provisions. He expressed his honor at hosting such an esteemed guest. Rama, in turn, acknowledged Guha's affection and hospitality, but declined the offerings, explaining his commitment to a life of asceticism, sustained by fruits, roots, and the bark of trees. He requested only fodder for his horses, emphasizing their importance as his father's beloved animals.  Guha immediately ordered his men to provide the horses with proper feed and drink. Rama, after performing evening rituals, consumed only water, observing a fast. Lakshmana washed Rama and Sita's feet before retiring to a nearby tree.  Guha, along with Sumantra, kept watch over the sleeping Rama, discussing his virtues.  Thus, the night passed for Rama, who, accustomed to comfort, now lay on the bare ground.

He declared his deep affection for Rama and pledged to protect him and Sita with his kinsmen.  Guha emphasized his familiarity with the forest and his ability to defend them against any threat.  Lakshmana declined the offer, explaining his inability to rest while his brother and sister-in-law slept on the ground.  He lamented their exile and expressed his concern for his father, King Dasaratha, and mothers, fearing they might not survive the grief. He pictured Ayodhya, once filled with cries of anguish, now fallen silent with exhaustion. He worried most about Queen Kausalya, believing his own mother, Sumitra, might find solace in the hope of seeing her other son, Shatrughna.

He imagined the lamentations of the women in the palace, now silenced by exhaustion. Lakshmana worried about Queen Kausalya, Rama's mother, and his own mother, Sumitra, though he believed Sumitra might find some comfort in the hope of seeing her other son, Shatrughna. He envisioned Ayodhya, once joyful and prosperous, now desolate and grieving.  He questioned how his father could endure the absence of his eldest son. Lakshmana predicted that if Dasaratha perished, Kausalya and then Sumitra would follow. He lamented that his father would die without seeing Rama ascend the throne.  He pictured the funeral rites, performed by those fortunate enough to survive.  Lakshmana then shifted to a more hopeful vision of Ayodhya, thriving and bustling with activity, should his father live. He expressed his wish that he and Rama would safely return from exile to this prosperous city.  Overwhelmed by grief and worry, Lakshmana continued to lament throughout the night. Witnessing Lakshmana's deep sorrow, Guha, too, wept.

__data__.text: Sri Rama, at daybreak, addressed Lakshmana, noting the sunrise and the sounds of cuckoos and peacocks, and proposed they cross the Ganga river. Lakshmana informed Guha, who promptly ordered a boat.  A minister quickly brought a suitable vessel to the riverbank and informed Guha. Guha, with folded hands, offered the boat to Rama, inquiring if he could offer further assistance.  Rama accepted, requesting everything be loaded quickly.  Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita, armed and armored, then proceeded towards the river.  The charioteer, Sumantra, asked Rama for further instructions.  Rama, touching Sumantra's hand, instructed him to return to Ayodhya and remain composed, explaining that they would continue their journey into the Dandaka forest on foot. Sumantra, distressed at being dismissed, made a final plea to Rama.

__data__.text: Sumantra, the charioteer, overcome with grief, questioned Rama about his own future now that Rama was leaving.  Rama instructed Sumantra to return swiftly to Ayodhya and remain composed. He reiterated his intent to journey to Dandaka forest on foot.  Sumantra, distraught, lamented Rama's exile, comparing it to the life of a common man. He questioned the value of piety and learning if even Rama could face such adversity.  He declared that despite the exile, Rama, accompanied by Sita and Lakshmana, would ultimately achieve glory. Sumantra then expressed his own despair at being left behind, fearing the influence of Kaikeyi.  Overwhelmed, Sumantra wept. Once composed, Rama consoled Sumantra, urging him to comfort Dasaratha and prevent him from grieving. He emphasized Sumantra’s importance as a friend to the Ikshvaku dynasty and instructed him to obey Dasaratha's commands, particularly those related to Kaikeyi, explaining that a king's purpose is to ensure his will is carried out.  Rama's final instruction was for Sumantra to respectfully convey a message to Dasaratha upon his return.

Kaikeyi, whose heart was poisoned by the malicious gossip of Manthara as
aforesaid, takes a vow to see that Rama is sent into exile and Bharata
installed as Prince Regent, and asks Manthara herself how to
secure that consummation. Manthara tells her how in the
course of a conflict between gods and demons, in which
Dasaratha’s help was enlisted by the gods, the queen,
who had accompanied her husband to the field of
operations and had rendered valuable assistance
to him at a critical juncture, was offered a couple
of boons, which she had kept in abeyance.

Manthara now asks Kaikeyi to demand the
banishment of Rama and the installation of
Bharata against the two promised boons.

Kaikeyi accordingly throws away her
ornaments and lies down on the bare
floor in the sulking-room in
a sullen mood

Enraged to hear the exhortation of Sri Rama, Laksmana urges in reply that
the word of their father was worth ignoring inasmuch as it was divorced
from righteousness and, further emphasizing the predominance

the imperative necessity of their carrying out
the command of their father

Canto XXXIV

Apprised of Sri Rama’s arrival by Sumantra, Dagaratha commands him to
usher in Sri Rama with his consort. Seeing the Emperor fall unconscious
at the very sight of the heir-apparent, the ladies of the royal household
start wailing piteously. On Sri Rama’s soliciting his permission to
retire to the woods, the king enjoins him to take his father
captive and ascend the throne. Sri Rama in his turn
consoles his father by assuring him that he has no
hankering for royal fortune and that to him
obedience to his father’s command is of
utmost importance. Dasaratha, however,
falls unconscious again at the very thought
of his separation from Sri Rama and
Sumantra as well as all the ladies of
the gynaeceum follow suit

at the very sight of the heir-apparent, the ladies of the royal household
start wailing piteously. On Sri Rama’s soliciting his permission to

falls unconscious again at the very thought
of his separation from Sri Rama and
Sumantra as well as all the ladies of
the gynaeceum follow suit

Canto XXXVI

DaSaratha instructs Sumantra to take a detachment of the army and the
exchequer alongwith Sri Rama, to which Kaikeyi objects and insists
on his being sent into exile without any resources on the analogy
of Asamafija, son of the king’s forefather, Sagara. Another minister
of the king, Siddhartha by name, who was present there, opposes
Kaikeyi and urges that the analogy of Asamafija, who was a
perverse lad, could not be applied in the case of Sri Rama,
who possessed an ideal character and deserved in every
way to be installed in the office of Prince Regent. In
the event of Kaikeyi vetoing the proposal, the king
threatens to accompany the heir-apparent

Canto XL

Going clockwise round DaSaratha (as a token of respect), Sita, Rama and
Laksmana greet him. Accompanied by Sita, Sri Rama salutes Kausalya.
Laksmana too hails Kausalya first and then his own mother, Sumitra.
Sumitra for her part tenders salutary advice to her son. The princes
and the princess having mounted the chariot, Sumantra flicks
the horses. The citizens that had assembled, closely follow
the chariot; but unable to keep pace with its swift
movement, they return desolate. Dasaratha too
runs after the chariot alongwith Kausalya
and others, but being unable to walk
begins to totter and stops short
on the road yielding to the
remonstrances of his
wise ministers

Canto XLII

Sri Rama having departed for the forest in an exceptionally swift-going
chariot, Dasaratha vainly seeks to cover the intervening distance on foot.
The very dust raised by the chariot having disappeared after a while,
the Emperor feels doubly disconsolate and drops to the ground.
When Kaikeyi comes forward to support him, he scolds her and
asks her not to touch his person. Kausalya then lifts him up
and persuades him to return. His personal attendants
take him to the latter's apartments and, seeing him
plunged in grief, Kausalya seats herself beside
him and begins to lament in various ways

Canto XLVI

Having reached the bank of the Tamasa and thinking of the plight of the
people of Ayodhya, Sri Rama lays himself down on a bed of leaves
bewailing the lot of his parents and feeling reassured by the thought
of Bharata’s noble qualities; while Laksmana opens his dialogue
with Sumantra on the divine excellences of Sri Rama. Waking
up in the meantime, Sri Rama urges the charioteer-minister to
drive the chariot in such a way as to put the citizens, that
had accompanied them, off the scent and lead them to
think that the chariot had turned back towards
Ayodhya instead of proceeding towards the forest.

He then mounts the chariot alongwith Sita and
Laksmana and presses on to the forest

Canto LI

Expressing his readiness to guard the Crown prince and his consort,
keeping awake the whole night, Guha importunes Laksmana to repose.
Reminding Guha of Sri Rama’s greatness, Laksmana, however, tells
him that even though the duty of guarding his princely brother and
his consort could as well be entrusted to Guha, he felt that he
did not deserve to lie down in the presence of his elder
brother and sister-in-law and preferred to remain awake.
Expressing grief for his royal father and loving mothers
he therefore spends the night talking with Guha

Canto LII

While about to step into the boat brought by Guha’s men and asked by Guha
if he could be of any further use to the prince, Sri Rama enjoins him to
obey the Emperor. Importuned by Sumantra to take him as a personal
attendant to the forest, the prince declines his loving offer and,
expostulating with him, sends him back to Ayodhya. Entangling
their locks into a thick mass with the milk of a banyan tree,
procured by Guha, Sri Rama and Laksmana with Sita
get into the boat. On reaching the middle of the
stream, Sita offers prayers to Mother Ganga
(the deity presiding over the stream) and
after crossing the river all the three halt

for the night at the foot of a tree
